UK experts16 have also published guidelines for the proph- ylaxis of malaria. In areas where P. falciparum is sensitive to chloroquine, travellers can either take chloroquine or proguanil for prophylaxis. In areas of little chloroquine re- sistance travellers can take chloroquine plus proguanil, while travellers to areas of high infection risk or where there is chloroquine resistance may take mefloquine, doxy- cycline, or atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) as prophy- laxis. Standby treatment with chloroquine is recommend- ed for travellers to chloroquine-sensitive areas who do not take any prophylaxis or who take proguanil as prophylax- is. Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone), artemether-lume- fantrine (Riamet), or quinine plus doxycycline are recom- mended in areas with chloroquine resistance. Malaria vaccines are under development and several are currently undergoing clinical evaluation (see p.2221). Prophylaxis during pregnancy. The choice of drugs for prophylaxis during pregnancy is limited and whenever possible women who are pregnant or likely to become so should avoid travelling to malarious areas (see also above). In pregnant women who cannot avoid travelling to endemic areas, chloroquine may be given alone for proph- ylaxis in the few areas where P. falciparum is sensitive to chloroquine, or with proguanil where resistance exists.2 Folate supplements (folic acid 5 mg daily) need to be taken with proguanil. Mefloquine is normally avoided during the first trimester but may be given during the second and third trimesters and CDC15 and UK16 guidelines consider that it may be used with caution in the first trimester, especially in areas where there is a high risk of acquiring falciparum malaria. Doxycycline, atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone), or primaquine are contra-indicated in pregnant women by most experts; the BNF considers that atovaquone-pro- guanil (Malarone) should be avoided during pregnancy unless there is no suitable alternative. In non-pregnant women of child-bearing potential, pregnancy needs to be avoided for 3 months after completing mefloquine prophy- laxis and for one week following doxycycline prophylaxis. For those living in endemic areas, WHO7 recommends that, in areas of stable transmission of P. falciparum malar- ia, pregnant women and their newborn should sleep under insecticide-treated nets; pregnant women should also be given intermittent preventative treatment (IPT) with an antimalarial drug, usually pyrimethamine-sulfadoxin
